s27.title: An Outlier's take on the '26 worlds strategic situation, post 3

s28.title: An Outlier's take on the '26 worlds strategic situation, post 5

bet.text: Capacity, throughput and a turret to go around defense: the team believed these matter most at the highest level of play.

demand.text: Fuel scoring and passing. The team made it able to shoot on the bump while under defense, and added a hood roller because the static hood could not shoot or pass very far.

auto.text: Autos are states that drive to points. Side cameras give a position as the robot crosses the bump, until the main Limelight can see tags.
When no partner took the outpost, an analyst saw one pass through the middle, a push along the hub wall, then scoring from the outpost.
The hub push collects fuel, with no odometry reset.

cycle.text: Intaking balls fill the robot from the rear and stay loosely packed, so it can shoot without gaps.
At Orange County an analyst saw it take opponents' fuel outside its shift, wait without collecting more, then go back to the middle for fuel it had just scored.
At the SoCal district championship it cycled the center while 3476 drew defense.

endgame.text: At Orange County an analyst saw it score from on the bump in the last seconds, after its alliance had left little fuel on its own side for the endgame.

fallback.text: After its alliance lost auto in Einstein finals 1, an analyst says it cleared the neutral zone during the transition shift instead of going back to score. The alliance lost that match with a partner disabled.

gave_up.text: Chamfered corners needed custom swerve plates, and the dye rotor forced a split drive rail with a tight battery fit. The flexible net could hide the tags from the main Limelight when full. Hood roller belts took much of the space for flywheel mass.

changed.text: The static hood used at Orange County and the district championship took a lot of current and could not shoot very far, so a hood roller was added before the world championship. So were two side cameras. The net, first zip-tied to the turret's top plate, got a slotted metal plate. The binder shows 10 rotor and 11 shooter versions.

outcome.text: 70-2-0 in official play; won the Daly division, won the championship; captain of the Daly alliance on Einstein; ranked 1 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 429.48, Daly).

solves.text: Maximize hopper area and dye rotor diameter within the frame perimeter, with the rotor kept low

facts.text: Frame size 25 x 32 in
Two custom swerve modules use WCP Swerve X2 components
The only custom module parts are three milled aluminum plates
Swerve gearing 7.67:1, to minimize current draw when accelerating
The left drive rail is split to move the battery to the edge; two cross rails provide structure to the dye rotor
To optimize swerve placement and hopper capacity the team printed empty shells to scale and filled them with BBs to estimate capacity
Electronics under the dye rotor are reached by turning the robot on its side
The plastic sheet under the electronics grew from 1/16 to 1/8 in; the stiffer sheet helped the robot slide off balls

cost.text: The battery is a very tight fit and needed some custom work; the team reported no problems with it

functions.name: Bumpers
functions.type: structural bumpers that form the hopper walls

solves.text: Gain hopper space and support the shooter with the bumper backing

facts.text: Extra hopper space per side, about
Mainly .090 in bent aluminum, with bent polycarbonate side panels reinforced with SRPP
3D printed stadium pieces funnel balls into the dye rotor
Only the bumpers and the dye rotor sit between the shooter and the robot, so the turret is somewhat free spinning when the bumpers are off
With the bumpers off the shooter wobbles only a little on the dye rotor alone
The cloth is riveted to the aluminum backing through holes made with a soldering iron

cost.text: Every bumper swap means removing about six turret plate bolts, then flexing and tilting the large section to get it off

functions.name: Intake
functions.type: linear extending roller intake with independent sides

solves.text: Survive impacts by collapsing at once, with no crash bar

facts.text: Primary 3 in polycarbonate roller powered by two Kraken X60s at 3.45:1
Bottom 1.5 in roller powered by one Kraken X44 at 1.5:1
The bottom roller is stored behind the front roller, drops on surgical tubing at the start of the match and is held by latches
Doubled .25 in polycarbonate gear racks act as leaf springs, with one Kraken X44 on each side
Each side slides independently and springs back out after a hit
The two rack plates are not bolted together, so they stay floppy; the unconstrained section above them, where hits usually land, is made rigid
Bearing stacks let it slide smoothly
A cable chain on one side feeds one intake motor, and wires across the front panel reach the other
Screws hold the roller tubes, since they do not slip or shear and make the regular changes of silicone rollers easier

cost.text: Rack teeth were starting to chip after the first event, when only one of the two plates had teeth; with teeth on both, none chipped or broke

functions.name: Extending hopper and net
functions.type: extending hopper with a flexible net

solves.text: Add capacity while the starting configuration stays under the trench

facts.text: Holds under the trench, at least
Holds over the bump with the net, at least
A season reviewer gives its hopper as 80 fuel
A slotted metal plate holds the net, and a plate below guards the turret gear
The front wall is SRPP for weight; the other walls are not, because the team cannot bend SRPP
A poster says chamfered corners make the netted hopper much bigger than drum-shooter hoppers, and that fuel kept inside it cannot be counterfed

cost.text: When full, the net could block the main Limelight's view of the hub tags, so two side cameras were added before the world championship

functions.name: Dye Rotor
functions.type: coaxially powered dye rotor with passive rollers

solves.text: Feed the shooter without jams or gaps

facts.text: Two Kraken X60s drive the rollers, with 2.5:1 on the feeder wheels, and one rotates the rotor at 36.4:1
Powered coaxially through a long belt and a reinforced gear train, not through a slip ring
Passive rollers let each ball push the one ahead up the tunnel and lower current draw
The vertical wheel sits inside the rotor, so balls settle in front of it with zero compression
A dolphin fin ramp on the outside of the slowly reversing rotor agitates balls and reduces packing pressure
A commenter says it indexed more slowly than 4946 but performed far better because it was short; another disputes that 4946 would have been better short
It spins at about 2.25 rev/s, or 20 balls/s in theory, much faster than first tested as optimal; balls slip on the passive rollers and leave without gaps at 12 to 14 balls/s
The shooter's feeder wheels are the main limit on ball rate; the rotor wheels run much faster
Motor speeds are 80 rev/s for the rotor and 90 rev/s for the rollers
Testing found it extremely critical that balls fall straight down into the rotor unobstructed
Brushes on a driven moving floor, meant to pull balls in faster and close gaps, were an early prototype; most moving-floor versions stayed in CAD
Its 32 mm goBILDA wheels are drilled out and broached to 3/8 in hex
Version 9 played at Ventura, Orange County and the district championship; version 10, with minor upgrades, played at the world championship

functions.name: Shooter
functions.type: geared flywheel with a powered hood roller

solves.text: Recover speed fast and shoot far from a compact turret

facts.text: Four Kraken X44s geared 1:1 to a 3 in flywheel
Three 1 in feeder wheels with .5 in compression, and a 1 in hood roller at half the surface speed
Every wheel in the shooter is geared together
Copper flywheels .25 in thick, plus copper discs inside the wheels
Two GT2 belts over the hood side plates drive the hood roller
Hood driven by one Kraken X44 at 85.3:1
All motors are stacked vertically so few parts protrude
The hood pivots on the same axis as the shooter wheels
The flywheel moved back to fit the Limelight in front inside the turret ring, which left 1.75 in of overhang
Aluminum parts that may take high impacts are 7075, as are all laser-cut 20 DP gears, for hardness
Version 6 played at Ventura, 8 at Orange County, 9 at the district championship and 11 at the world championship

functions.name: Turret
functions.type: compact turret on an X-contact bearing

solves.text: Go around defense, in little height

facts.text: One Kraken X44 at 55.7:1
The X-contact bearing is shared by the dye rotor and the shooter
A sliding flex-wheel tensioner with two 8 lb constant force springs takes up the cable chain
Height of the turret and cable chain stack-up, less than
The cable chain wraps around four printed guides and joins the turret with two short bolts that let it flip 180 degrees as the turret passes over the center
Constant tension matters when the turret whips around: without it the chain snags and breaks links
During championship qualification a poster put the time it spent in its alliance zone without shooting, lost to aligning and driving, at about 0.5 s, against 3 s for 254
The shooter rests mainly on the X-contact bearing above the dye rotor; bearing stacks at the turret plate on the bumpers add radial support

cost.text: The team tried running the turret Limelight on both Ethernet and HDMI to shrink the turret's swept volume; it fried a couple of Limelights and advises against it

functions.name: Software
functions.type: precomputed shot map with tilt compensation

solves.text: Shoot and feed while moving, tilted or under defense

facts.text: For a range of distances and robot velocities it computes all possible scoring shots beforehand and finds the one most robust to errors
Shots simulated in one sweep for the hub, about
A second-order polynomial looks up hood angle and flywheel speed at runtime; the turret compensates for tangential velocity
Robot pitch and yaw correct the shot so it can shoot on the bump
One Limelight that always points at the hub does about 95 percent of localization; two side cameras help when it cannot see tags
Fully state-machine based, with no commands
Saved gyro and turret angles turn each tag estimate into a robot pose, which is dropped unless it is on the field, about flat and not moving or turning too fast
The shot solver follows a 2022 talk by 1690, but finds every shot between the close and far rim to measure how tolerant each one is
Shots are tuned in two steps: a constant hood offset from slow-motion video, then one constant from wheel speed to ball speed, adjusted slightly as balls wear in
Wheel speed to ball speed was near linear for most shooter versions; one needed a small lookup table
Feeding has its own maps: a low shot with little bounce and one over the back of the net
An AI summary of the code, posted by the team, says tilt compensation acts above 2 degrees of tilt and is off during a shoot-on-the-fly lockout
The binder says people review what AI agents attempt; the tilt compensation code was not reviewed by a person

cost.text: Two USB ports failed on the Orange Pi that runs two PhotonVision cameras on the turret plate, perhaps from static, so the championship playoffs were run with one; problems like this are part of why the turret camera is a Limelight

decisions.because: iteration found it the most consistent and accurate setup, which surprised the team
decisions.instead_of: an independent feeder that regulates speed before the flywheel

decisions.choice: Change from command-based code to state machines
decisions.because: command-based code caused loop overruns and was harder to debug
decisions.cost: many open-source auto tools rely on commands and no longer fit well, so the team built its own framework around driving to points

decisions.choice: Add a hood roller between the district and world championships
decisions.because: the static hood took a lot of current and could not shoot or pass very far
decisions.cost: its belts took space for flywheel inertia

decisions.because: the hood roller belts left little space and copper is slightly denser than steel

decisions.choice: Chamfer the back corners with custom swerve modules
decisions.because: balls pack better than in square corners and the drive base is larger for the same perimeter
decisions.cost: custom module plates and difficult packaging around the dye rotor

decisions.choice: Extend the bumpers into hopper walls
decisions.because: newer bumper rules allow about an inch and a half of hard parts beyond the frame, and a dye rotor can use extra space on three sides

decisions.choice: Thick polycarbonate front roller with no crash bar
decisions.because: it needs no sacrificial material in front and helps compliance; the team worried that a beater bar could collapse inward and stall the roller

decisions.choice: Cut the turret gear at 20 DP
decisions.because: it doubles the ratio available compared with 10 DP, so the gearbox is compact

decisions.choice: Write fully state-machine code with no commands
decisions.because: it is easier to reason about for the AI agents that attempt features

decisions.choice: Take the whole bumper hopper off to change colors
decisions.because: swapping only the foam, fabric and thin metal backing could not be made to work cleanly in time; in hindsight removing it all gave better access for inspection and repairs
decisions.instead_of: a hopper part fixed to the robot with a swapped cover

decisions.choice: One gear-driven motor for each intake side
decisions.because: it removed the risk of belt slip, and one side can collapse in a hit while the other stays out; packaging around the dye rotor was the first reason to consider it
decisions.instead_of: one motor and a belt-driven jackshaft, whose belts could slip on impact in testing

decisions.because: the team worried that SRPP would deform for good after a huge impact, delaminate or wear faster at the teeth
decisions.instead_of: SRPP racks, held as a fallback if polycarbonate broke

decisions.choice: X-contact bearings in the dye rotor
decisions.because: their clamps are very low profile and they are smoother and more rigid

decisions.choice: Bearing stacks at the turret plate
decisions.because: the first shooter needed an X-contact bearing there too large to source, and the stacks package well with the turret gear, keeping the cable chain high

decisions.choice: No absolute encoder on the turret
decisions.because: the Limelight turns with it and its tag estimates correct the gyro zero, so the turret points at the goal; it is zeroed by eye
decisions.cost: the gyro zero is thrown off, by about a degree that a driver likely does not notice; the team says this is not the best way, but that vision would not gain it points this season

decisions.because: MegaTag 2 and hybrid approaches gave minimal gains compared with a well-placed camera aimed at the main point of interest

decisions.choice: Tune a simulated shot map with one ball speed constant
decisions.because: it was built before the robot ran, cut tuning time, and one small change corrects the full range of shots, though the team does not claim the best shot of the season
decisions.instead_of: a lookup map tuned by hand at every distance

decisions.choice: One depot auto with a single bump crossing for the championship
decisions.because: it gave the most shooting time, let the robot end in the center, worth perhaps 30 to 40 balls, and worked with any partner or placement
decisions.instead_of: a double sweep, which scored less
decisions.cost: without four strong robots rushing the middle, the fuel behind the hub does not collect into a triangle

decisions.choice: Block CAD as a 3-dimensional master sketch
decisions.because: it shows packaging, collisions and space claims without holes or plate outlines, so changes stay simple; each plate in detail CAD is sketched on its block
decisions.instead_of: Krayola CAD, which was not detailed enough
